items.question: How do you reflect on the progress of language-model coding since the first signs you saw in GPT-3?
items.object: Early language-model coding capabilities and adaptation to their progress
items.answer: Well, I remember back in the GPT-3 days seeing the very first signs of life of take a doc string, a Python definition of a function name, and then watching the model complete the code. And as soon as you saw that, you knew this is going to work. This is going to be big. And I remember at some point we were talking about these aspirational goals of imagine if you could have a language model that would write a thousand lines of coherent code, right? That was like a big goal for us. And the thing that's kind of wild is that that goal has come and passed. And I think that we don't think twice about it, right? I think that while you're developing this technology, you really just see the holes, the flaws, the things that don't work. But every so often, it's good to step back and realize that actually things have just come so far. It's incredible how used we get to things improving all the time and how to just become a daily driver. You just use it every day and then you reflect back to a month ago. This wasn't even possible. And this just continues to happen. I think that's quite fascinating, how quickly humans adapt to new things.

items.question: How do you see OpenAI's concentrated focus on coding fitting into its pursuit of general intelligence?
items.object: Coding as a specialized focus within OpenAI's pursuit of general intelligence
items.answer: Now, one of the struggles that we've always had is the question of whether to go deep in a domain, right? Because we're really here for the G, for AGI, general intelligence. And so to first order, our instinct is just push on making all the capabilities better at once. Coding has always been the exception to that, right? We really have a very different program that we use to focus on coding data, on code metrics, on trying to really understand how our models perform on code. And, you know, we've started to do that in other domains, too. But for programming and coding, that's been a very exceptional focus for us. And, you know, for GPT-4, we really produced a single model that was just a leap on all fronts. But we actually had trained the Codex model. And I remember doing a Python sort of focused model. Like, we were really, really trying to push the level of coding capability back in 2021 or so.

items.question: What did building the early Codex demo teach you about making coding models useful?
items.object: The harness and practical usability of coding models
items.answer: And I remember when we did the Codex demo, that was maybe the first demonstration of what we'd call Vibe coding today. I remember building this interface and having this realization that for just standard language model stuff, the interface, the harness, is so simple. You're just completing a thing and maybe there's a follow-up turn or something like that. But that's it. For coding, this text comes to life, right? You need to execute it, that it needs to be hooked up to tools, all these things. And so you realize that the harness is almost equally part of how you make this model usable as the intelligence. And so that is something that I think we kind of knew from that moment. And it's been interesting to see as we got to more capable models this year and really started to focus on not just making the raw capability, like how do you win at programming competitions, but how do you make it useful, right? Training in a diversity of environments, really connecting to how people are going to use it, and then really building the harness, which is something that Thibaut and his team have really pushed hard.

items.question: What did working on GitHub Copilot teach you about latency as a product feature?
items.object: Latency in GitHub Copilot's autocomplete interface
items.answer: The thing that was very interesting there was that for the first time you really felt what is it like to have an AI in the middle of your coding workflow and how can it accelerate you. And I remember that there were a lot of questions around the exact right interface. Do you want ghost text so it just does a completion? Do you want a little dropdown with a bunch of different possibilities? But one thing that was very clear was latency was a product feature. And the constraint for something like an autocomplete is that 1,500 milliseconds, right? That's like the time that you have to produce a completion. Anything slower than that, it could be incredibly brilliant. No one wants to sit around waiting for it. And so the mandate that we had, the clear signal we had from users and from the product managers and all the people thinking about the product side of it, is get the smartest model you can subject to the latency constraint.

items.question: How do you think coding interfaces should adapt to smarter AI models that exceed an existing latency budget?
items.object: Adapting coding interfaces to smarter but slower AI models
items.answer: And then you have something like GPT-4, which is much, much smarter, but it's not going to hit your latency budget. What do you do? Is it a useless model? Absolutely not. The thing you have to do is you change the harness, you change the interface. And I think that that's a really important theme: you need to co-evolve the interfaces and the way that you use the model around its affordances. And so super fast, smart models are going to be great, but the incredibly smart but slower models, it's also worth it. And I think that we've always had a thesis that the returns on that intelligence are worth it. And it's never obvious in the moment because you're just like, well, it's just going to be too slow. Why would anyone want to use it? But I think that our approach has very much been to say that the greater intelligence will pan out in the long run.

items.question: How do you think about the balance between intelligence and convenience when making AI tools useful?
items.object: The balance between intelligence and convenience in AI tools
items.answer: I remember at the beginning of the year talking to one of our engineers, who I think is really fantastic. And he was saying that ChatGPT, we had this integration where it could automatically see the context in this terminal. And he's like, it's transformative because he doesn't have to copy-paste errors. He just can instantly be like, hey, what's the bug? And it would just tell him, and it was great. And you realize that it was an integration that we built that was so transformative. It wasn't about a smarter model. And I think that one thing that's very easy to get confused by is to really focus on only one of these dimensions and be like, which one matters? Because the answer is they kind of both matter. And the way I've always thought about this, I remember when we were originally releasing the API back in 2020, is there are two dimensions to what makes an AI desirable. There's intelligence, which you can think of as one axis. And then there's convenience, which you can think of as latency. You could think of as cost. You could think of as the integrations available to it. And there's some acceptance region, right? Where it's like, if the model's incredibly smart, but it takes you a month to run it or something, you still might, right? If what's going to output is such a valuable piece of code or cure for a certain disease or something like that, okay, fine, it's worthwhile. If the model is not that intelligent, not that capable, then all you want to do is autocomplete. So it has to be incredibly convenient, zero cognitive tax for you to think about what it's suggesting, that kind of thing. And where we are is, of course, somewhere on the spectrum now. We now have smarter models that are reasonably less convenient than autocomplete, but still more convenient than you have to sit around and wait for a month for the answer to appear. And so I think that a lot of our challenge is figuring out when do you invest in pulling that convenience to the left? When do you invest in pushing the intelligence up? And it's a massive design space. It's what makes it fun.

items.question: How do you think about OpenAI's priorities in an increasingly competitive AI landscape?
items.object: OpenAI's priorities in the competitive AI landscape
items.answer: I focus a little less on the competition and a little more on the potential, right? Because we started OpenAI in 2015 thinking that AGI is going to be possible, maybe sooner than people think. And we just want to be a positive force in how it plays out, right? And really thinking about what does that mean, trying to connect that to practical execution has been a lot of the task. And so as we started to figure out how to build capable models that are actually useful, that can actually help people, actually bringing that to people is this really critical thing. And you can look at choices that we've made along the way, for example, releasing ChatGPT and making the ChatGPT free tier available widely. That's something that we do because of our mission, because we really think about wanting AI to be available and accessible and benefit everyone. And so in my view, the most important thing is to continue on that exponential progress and really think about how to bring it to people in a positive and useful way.

items.question: How do you understand the role of reinforcement learning and tool use in making coding models more capable?
items.object: Reinforcement learning and tool use for coding models
items.answer: So I really look at where we're at right now: there's the GPT-4 class of pre-trained models. There's reinforcement learning on top of it to make it much more reliable and smart. It's like, if you've just sort of read the internet, you've just observed a bunch of human thought, and you're trying to write some code for the first time, you're probably going to have a bad time of it. But if you've had the ability to actually try to solve some hard code problems, you have a Python interpreter, you have access to the kinds of tools that humans do, then you're going to be able to become much more robust and refined. So we now have these pieces working together in concert, but we've got to keep pushing them to the next level.

items.question: Why do you see AI-assisted refactoring of massive code bases as such a significant opportunity?
items.object: AI-assisted refactoring of massive code bases
items.answer: It's very clear that things like being able to refactor massive code bases, no one's cracked that just yet. There's no fundamental reason we can't. And I think the moment you get that, refactoring code is one of the killer use cases for enterprise, right? If you could bring down the cost of code migrations by 2x, I think you'll end up with 10x more of them happening. Think about the number of systems that are stuck in COBOL. And there's no COBOL programmers being trained, right? It's strictly building liability for the world to have this dependency. The only way through is by building systems that can tackle that. So I just think it's a massive open space. The exponential continues and we need to stay on that.

items.question: How do you assess the progress of AI code review beyond models trying to defend their mistakes?
items.object: AI code review and progress beyond doubling down on mistakes
items.answer: Oh, yeah. It would try to convince you that it was right. We're so far past that being the core problem. I'm sure it happens in some obscure edge cases, just like it does for humans. But it's really amazing to see that we're at a level where even when it's not quite zeroed in on the right thing, it's highlighting stuff that matters. It has pretty reasonable thoughts. And I always walk away from these code reviews thinking, huh, okay, yeah, that's a good point. I should be thinking about that.

items.question: How do you see AI coding agents changing the value of your work as an engineer?
items.object: AI coding agents and the value of programmers
items.answer: I get to do more. It's like, is what I want to spend my time doing, is what I want people to know me for, being able to find functionality in the code base? Absolutely not. That's not how I define my value as an engineer, what I want to spend my time on as an engineer. And now I think that that to me is the core of it, right? That there's this amazing intelligence and that it can, first of all, suck away all the mundane, boring parts. And certainly some of the fun parts too, right? I think that really thinking about the architecture of things, it's a great partner. But I get to choose how I spend my time. And I get to think about how many of these agents you want running on what tasks, how do I break down things? And so I view it as increasing the opportunity surface for programmers.

items.question: What makes AI coding assistance in your terminal valuable enough to become part of how you work?
items.object: AI coding assistance in the terminal
items.answer: I'm an Emacs user through and through. I started using VS Code and Cursor and Windsurf and these things, partly to try things out, but partly because I like the diversity of different tools, but it's really hard to get me out of my terminal. But I have found that we're now above threshold where I really find myself missing the—I'm doing some refactor, and I'm like, why am I typing this thing? You're trying to remember exactly the syntax for a specific thing or do these very mechanical things. I'm like, I just want to have an intern go do the thing. But I have that now in my terminal. And I think it's really amazing that we're at the point that you have this core intelligence and that you get to pick and choose when and how to use it.

items.question: How do you think AI could change the cat-and-mouse game between cybersecurity attackers and defenders?
items.object: AI and the attacker-defender dynamic in cybersecurity
items.answer: The way that it's always worked is that there's a cat and mouse game between attackers getting more sophisticated, defenders getting better. And I think that with AI, you're like, well, maybe it's going to— which side will advantage the most? Maybe it'll just accelerate this cat and mouse. But I think that there's some hope that actually you can unlock fundamental new capabilities through AI, for example, formal verification, that are sort of an end game for defense. And I think that that to me is very exciting: thinking about not just how do you continue this never-ending rat race, but how do you actually end up with increased stability, increased understandability? And I think that there's other opportunities like that for us to really understand our systems in a way that right now we're at the edge of human understanding of the traditional software systems that have been built.

items.question: What do you want Codex to achieve for software engineering?
items.answer: One of the reasons we built Codex is to improve the infrastructure and the code out there in the world, not necessarily to increase the amount of code in the world. And so this is a very important point where it's also helping find bugs, helping refactor, helping find more elegant, more performant implementations that achieve the same thing or actually are more general, but not necessarily ending up with 100 million lines of code that you don't understand. One thing that I'm really excited about is how Codex can help teams, individuals, just write better code, be better software engineers, and end up with simpler systems that are actually doing more things for us.

items.question: How do you see compute availability shaping an AI-enabled world of material abundance by 2030?
items.object: Material abundance and compute scarcity in the 2030 outlook
items.answer: I think part of the 2030 outlook is we will be in a world of material abundance. I think that AI is going to make it much easier than you could almost imagine to create anything you want. And that will probably be true in the physical world in addition to the digital world in ways that are hard to predict. But I think it will be a world of absolute compute scarcity. And we've seen a little bit of what this is like within OpenAI. The way that different research projects fight over compute or that the success of the research program is determined by the compute allocation is hard to overstate. And I think that we're going to be in a world where your ability to produce and create whatever you imagine will be limited partly by your imagination, but partly by the compute power behind it. And so one thing we think about a lot is how do we increase the supply of compute in the world? We want to increase the intelligence, but also the availability of that intelligence. And fundamentally, it is a physical infrastructure problem, not just a software problem. I know with GPT-5, one thing that's quite amazing is we're able to give it as part of the free, the Plus plan, the Pro plan. It's like you can use Codex with your Plus plan. You get GPT-5, the same version that everyone else gets. And it's this incredible intelligence. But the model is also incredibly cost-effective in that way.

The way that different research projects fight over compute or that the success of the research program is determined by the compute allocation is hard to overstate. And I think that we're going to be in a world where your ability to produce and create whatever you imagine will be limited partly by your imagination, but partly by the compute power behind it.

And so one thing we think about a lot is how do we increase the supply of compute in the world? We want to increase the intelligence, but also the availability of that intelligence. And fundamentally, it is a physical infrastructure problem, not just a software problem. I know with GPT-5, one thing that's quite amazing is we're able to give it as part of the free, the Plus plan, the Pro plan. It's like you can use Codex with your Plus plan. You get GPT-5, the same version that everyone else gets. And it's this incredible intelligence. But the model is also incredibly cost-effective in that way.
